name: Design an Event Streaming Platform
intent: Build a Kafka-style platform that carries millions of events per second as replicated, partitioned, append-only logs, which many teams write to and read from at their own pace, replay at will, and trust not to lose or duplicate.
codeTitle: idempotent producers, consumer-group offsets and compaction on a partitioned log
finalIntro: One event from a producer to a replicated partition and on to a consumer group.
prompt: Design a company-wide event streaming platform. Hundreds of services publish events such as orders, clicks and payments to named topics, and many other services and data jobs read them, some within milliseconds and some days later, and some to rebuild their state from the start. It must take about 500,000 events per second at the peak, keep the order of events for the same key, not lose an acknowledged event when a machine dies, let a group of consumers share one topic, and keep a week of history.
functional: Producers publish events to a topic, optionally with a key
Events with the same key are read in the order they were written
Consumers in one group share a topic's work, and every group sees every event
A group's position is remembered, so it resumes after a restart, and it can rewind to replay
Events are kept for a set time or size, and some topics keep only the latest event per key
A producer can write to several partitions atomically, and a retry never creates a duplicate
Teams get quotas, and event formats are checked when they are published
nonFunctional: About 500,000 events per second and 500 MB/s in at the peak, with a few groups reading each topic
Publishing takes under 20 ms at the 99th percentile when the replicas are healthy
An acknowledged event survives the loss of any one machine, and a whole zone when spread over three
Tens of thousands of partitions and hundreds of topics on one cluster
Reading an old event is as easy as reading a new one, and a slow reader never slows the writers
The cluster is rolled and repaired without stopping producers and consumers

firstAttempt.text: One SQL table of events with an auto-increment id. Producers insert rows, and each consumer polls for rows with an id above the last one it handled, and stores that id itself. Old rows are deleted by a nightly job.
limits: Hundreds of thousands of inserts per second hit one table and one index on one machine
Auto-increment ids are assigned before the commit, so a poller can skip a row that commits late and never see it
Each consumer polls constantly, and a hundred consumers mean a hundred queries over the same hot rows
Nothing shares the work between copies of one consumer, so they either all handle a row or need their own locking
Deleting old rows by query fights with the inserts, and a single machine cannot hold a week of data

steps.title: Replace the table with an append-only log
steps.problem: A database table that is both inserted into and polled is a poor queue: it needs random writes and indexes, readers fight the writers, and an id that is assigned before commit can make a reader skip a row for ever.
steps.fix: Give each topic a log, a file on the broker's disk that is only ever appended to. Each event gets the next offset, a number that grows by one, and is written sequentially and flushed in batches, which disks and the operating system's page cache do very well. A reader asks for 'everything from offset N' and the broker returns a range straight from the file. The log is cut into segment files so old ones can be dropped as a whole, and reading does not remove anything, so any number of readers can use the same data.
steps.tradeoff: Sequential writes and reads make hundreds of megabytes per second per machine ordinary, and readers cannot disturb the writers. The log has no random access by anything but offset or time, and a reader that wants 'events about customer 7' has to read them all or use another system.

steps.title: Split a topic into partitions, and choose the partition by key
steps.problem: One log lives on one machine, so one topic is limited by one disk and one network card, and only one reader at a time can keep its order.
steps.fix: A topic becomes many partitions, each its own log, spread over the brokers. The producer hashes the key to pick the partition, so all events for one customer or order are in the same partition, and order is guaranteed within a partition and not across them. Throughput grows by adding partitions, and clients learn which broker leads which partition from cluster metadata, then talk to that broker directly.
steps.tradeoff: A topic can grow with the cluster and per-key order is kept. There is no order between partitions, a very hot key makes a hot partition, and changing the partition count later changes where keys go, so it is chosen with room to grow.

steps.title: Share the work with consumer groups and committed offsets
steps.problem: Many applications read the same topic, and each wants to scale out over several copies without handling an event twice or forgetting where it was.
steps.fix: Each application is a consumer group (a set of copies of one application that share a topic). The group coordinator gives every partition to exactly one member of the group, so the members split the work while per-key order holds. Different groups are independent and each get every event. A member records how far it has processed by committing an offset, which is written to an internal compacted topic, and after a restart or a hand-over to another member the partition resumes there. When members join, leave or stop sending heartbeats, the partitions are reassigned in a rebalance.
steps.tradeoff: Each group scales to as many members as there are partitions and resumes where it stopped. Committing after processing means a crash repeats the last batch, which is at-least-once delivery, so handlers must tolerate repeats, and a rebalance briefly pauses the group.

steps.title: Replicate each partition, and acknowledge only what is safely copied
steps.problem: A partition on one machine is lost with that machine, and an acknowledged event must never disappear.
steps.fix: Every partition has a replication factor, usually three, in different zones. One replica is the leader and takes all reads and writes, and the followers fetch from it like any reader. The in-sync replicas (ISR) are the followers that are fully caught up. An event is committed, and visible to consumers, once every ISR member has it, and that point is the high watermark. With acks=all and a minimum of two in-sync replicas, a write is acknowledged only after two copies exist. If the leader dies, the controller elects a new leader from the ISR only.
steps.tradeoff: An acknowledged event survives one lost machine, and a fast leader is never held back by a dead follower for long, since it is dropped from the ISR. A producer waits for the slowest ISR member, and if too few replicas are in sync, writes are refused rather than risked, so availability is traded for safety.

steps.title: Make producers safe to retry, and write atomically across partitions
steps.problem: When an acknowledgement is lost, the producer cannot tell if the event was stored, and a retry either duplicates it or, with several requests in flight, reorders it. Stream processors also need to read, write results and commit offsets as one unit.
steps.fix: Each producer gets an id and numbers its batches per partition. The leader remembers the last sequence number for each producer and drops a repeat, which it still acknowledges, and refuses a gap, so retries create neither duplicates nor disorder, even with five requests in flight. For atomic writes across partitions, a transaction coordinator keeps a transaction log, the producer writes to its partitions and the coordinator then writes commit markers to all of them. Consumers set read-committed and skip events from open or aborted transactions.
steps.tradeoff: Exactly-once inside the platform costs very little for idempotence and more for transactions, which add extra round trips and markers and delay what a read-committed consumer can see. It does not cover side effects outside the platform, such as an email or a call to another service, which still need their own idempotency.

steps.title: Expire, compact and tier the history
steps.problem: A week of 500 MB/s is hundreds of terabytes, and some topics are not a stream of facts at all but the current state of each key, which must be kept for ever without keeping every past version.
steps.fix: Retention is set per topic. Time or size retention drops whole segments once they are old enough. A compacted topic keeps at least the latest event for every key, the cleaner rewrites old segments to remove superseded events, and a delete marker (a null value, called a tombstone) removes a key. Tiered storage moves closed segments to cheap object storage while recent ones stay on local disks, so a consumer can replay months of history without the brokers holding it.
steps.tradeoff: Disks stay small and a new service can rebuild its state from the topic. Compaction is eventual, so a reader may still see several old values before the cleaner runs, and a read from the cold tier is slower and uses network bandwidth.

steps.title: Run it as a shared platform: controller, schemas and quotas
steps.problem: The cluster needs a reliable source of truth about who leads what, and when hundreds of teams share it, one bad producer or one changed event format can hurt everyone.
steps.fix: A small controller quorum of three or five nodes runs a consensus protocol over a metadata log, which records topics, partitions, leaders and ISRs, and pushes changes to the brokers. A schema registry stores each topic's event schema and rejects a new version that breaks compatibility with the old, so producers and consumers can be deployed independently. Per-client quotas on bytes per second and request rate stop one team from using all the bandwidth, and ACLs control who can read and write each topic.
steps.tradeoff: One cluster is cheaper to run and easy to discover, and a bad actor is contained. Schema checks slow teams who want to change formats freely, quotas need tuning, and one shared cluster is a shared blast radius, so large companies split by criticality or region.

failures.scenario: A partition leader's machine dies in the middle of writes
failures.impact: Producers get errors for that partition, and events that were only on the dead leader are at risk.
failures.answer: The controller notices the missed heartbeats and elects a new leader from the in-sync replicas, which hold every committed event. Producers refresh the metadata and retry, and idempotent sequence numbers stop the retries from duplicating anything. Events that were never committed were never acknowledged under acks=all, so nothing acknowledged is lost. An unclean election of an out-of-sync replica would restore availability but could lose acknowledged events, so it is off by default.

failures.scenario: A follower falls behind and drops out of the in-sync set
failures.impact: With only the leader and one other replica in sync, one more failure makes the partition refuse writes.
failures.answer: The follower is removed from the ISR when it lags beyond the allowed time, so it stops slowing commits. With a minimum of two in-sync replicas, writes continue while two copies exist and stop with an error when only one is left, which turns a risk of data loss into a visible failure. The follower catches up from the leader, rejoins the ISR, and an alert fires when under-replicated partitions stay above zero.

failures.scenario: A consumer takes too long to process a batch and is removed from the group
failures.impact: A rebalance moves its partitions to others, the slow member's late commit is rejected, and the batch is processed twice.
failures.answer: Processing time and heartbeat are separate timeouts, so the group can tell a slow member from a dead one. The batch size and the maximum time between polls are tuned to the work, and handlers are idempotent so that a repeat does no harm. Cooperative rebalancing moves only the partitions that must move, so the rest of the group keeps working.

failures.scenario: One key is far hotter than the others
failures.impact: Its partition's leader and its single consumer are saturated, while the other partitions are idle.
failures.answer: Order is per key, so one key cannot be split without giving up its order. Options are to add a suffix to the key when order for that key does not matter, to put the heavy producer on its own topic, or to make the consumer batch and parallelise its work inside the partition by sub-key. Per-partition lag and byte metrics show the skew early.

failures.scenario: A bad event keeps crashing the consumer
failures.impact: The consumer fails, restarts from the committed offset, reads the same event and fails again, so the partition is stuck.
failures.answer: After a few attempts the consumer sends the event to a dead-letter topic with the error, commits past it, and carries on. Someone looks at the dead-letter topic, fixes the code or the data, and replays the events. The schema registry prevents a large class of these by rejecting malformed events at publish time.

alternatives.title: What delivery guarantee to build on

options.name: At-most-once
options.pro: Fastest and simplest: commit first, then process

options.name: At-least-once with idempotent handlers
options.pro: Nothing is lost and it works with any outside system
options.con: Every handler must cope with repeats

options.name: Exactly-once with transactions
options.pro: Read, process, write and commit offsets as one unit inside the platform
options.con: Extra latency and complexity, and it stops at the platform's edge

alternatives.pick: At-least-once as the default, with idempotent producers always on, and transactions for stream jobs that write back to the platform.

alternatives.title: How consumers get the data

options.name: Consumers pull ranges
options.pro: Each consumer sets its own pace, batches well and can rewind
options.con: An empty topic needs long polling to avoid wasted requests

options.name: The broker pushes events
options.pro: Slightly lower latency on a quiet topic
options.con: The broker must track every consumer's speed, and a slow one is overwhelmed or blocks others

alternatives.pick: Pull with long polling, so a slow consumer only falls behind and never hurts others.

alternatives.title: How much history to keep

options.name: Short time retention
options.con: A consumer that is down longer than that loses events, and no replays

options.name: Compaction
options.pro: Keeps the latest state per key for ever in bounded space
options.con: Past versions are gone, so it is for state and not for a full history

options.name: Long retention with tiered storage
options.pro: Replay of months of history from cheap storage
options.con: Cold reads are slow and storage costs grow with the history

alternatives.pick: A week locally for ordinary topics, compaction for state topics, and tiered storage where replay matters.

alternatives.title: Where the cluster metadata lives

options.name: A separate coordination service
options.con: A second system to run, with its own limits on how many partitions the cluster can have

options.name: A controller quorum inside the brokers
options.pro: One system, metadata as a log, fast failover and many more partitions
options.con: The platform owns its own consensus code

alternatives.pick: A built-in controller quorum, since it scales to far more partitions and removes a dependency.

roles.description: The brokers and the schema registry that producers talk to.

roles.label: Partition logs
roles.description: The append-only logs that hold events in order.

roles.label: Coordinators and consumers
roles.description: Consumer groups, the transaction coordinator and the controller quorum.

roles.label: Storage and offsets
roles.description: Replicas, committed offsets and tiered storage.

quiz.question: A SQL events table uses an auto-increment id and consumers poll 'where id > last_seen'. Transaction A takes id 100 but commits after transaction B, which took id 101. A consumer reads 101, stores last_seen = 101, and never sees 100. Which design removes this problem for good?
options: Poll with 'id > last_seen - 1000' and skip ids already handled, so any late commit is picked up on one of the next polls and nothing is skipped.
Replace the id with the commit timestamp and poll 'time > last_seen', so the ordering follows the clock of the database server.
Run the inserting transactions at SERIALIZABLE isolation, so ids are committed in the order they were taken.
An append-only log where the broker gives each event the next offset on append, so a reader from offset N misses nothing.
quiz.explanation: In a log the order is decided when the event is appended, not before a later commit, so a reader cannot skip one. A look-back window only hides the gap for a while and forces de-duplication. Timestamps have the same late-commit problem, and serialisable inserts would throttle writes to roughly one at a time.

quiz.question: Peak ingest on a streaming platform is 500 MB/s. Assume that rate were sustained for a whole week, with no compression and a replication factor of 3. About how much disk does the cluster need to keep a week of history?
options: About 130 TB, which is one day of data at 500 MB/s stored on three replicas
About 900 TB: 500 MB/s for a week is about 300 TB, and replication factor 3 stores it three times
About 300 TB, because the replicas of a partition are copies of the same data and take no extra space
About 1.2 PB, because replication factor 3 means the leader plus three more replicas, four copies in all
quiz.explanation: 500 MB/s is about 43 TB per day, about 300 TB per week, and replication factor 3 triples it to roughly 900 TB. Forgetting the replicas gives 300 TB, which is the usual mistake. A single day with three copies is about 130 TB, and the replication factor counts the leader, so there are three copies, not four. Because the peak is an upper bound and a week locally is costly, tiered storage moves old segments to cheap object storage.

quiz.question: A topic has replication factor 3, producers use acks=all, and min.insync.replicas is 2. Two followers of one partition die, so the in-sync set holds only the leader. What happens to this partition?
options: The leader keeps accepting writes, because acks=all only waits for the current in-sync set, and that set is now only the leader itself.
The controller promotes an out-of-sync replica, so writes can continue on a copy that lags behind.
Writes to it are refused while the leader still serves committed events, so no acknowledged data is put at risk.
The partition goes offline completely, and consumers can no longer read events that were already committed.
quiz.explanation: With a minimum of two in-sync replicas, a write needs two copies before it is acknowledged, so with one left the leader refuses it. That trades availability for safety. The leader alone would accept writes only if the minimum were 1, electing an out-of-sync replica could lose acknowledged events, and the leader still serves reads of committed events, so the partition is not offline.
